newsitem.title: GREECE: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK FINANCIAL NEWS - JAN 20.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK FINANCIAL NEWS - JAN 20.

text.p: Leading stories in the Greek financial press:

--An emergency meeting called today for the government's economic team will examine the alarming downturn in state revenues over recent months. The meeting will be the second in five days on the issue and will deal with the disappointingly low rates expected to continue this month, following a 2.0 percent fall in December. The government hopes to increase rates by 16 percent in the first quarter.

--The fall in interest rates and the rise of the Athens Stock Exchange has made mutual funds share values far more attractive, with returns running at 14 percent since the beginning of the year. Stricter controls on short selling is expected to further improve prospects.

--The judicial investigation into last year's Delta Securities scandal on the Athens Stock Exchange is now at a critical stage with the net closing in on those directly and indirectly involved. Leading players in the scandal have already been called to testify while the recent audit on all ASE members, sources say, has thrown much more light on the matter. The audit into Delta's books is expected to be completed soon and will be submitted to the authorities in early February.

--Thousands of National Bank customers with debts ranging from 10-200 million drachmas will be able to take advantage of new efforts to reschedule outstanding debts. The bank is aiming at putting an end to as many outstanding cases as it can. The new terms are expected to be effective as of next month, sources say, and will be far more favourable than in the past.

--The staffs of Greek banks have shown an ever-increasing upward trend in comparison to trends in other European countries. The two biggest state banks - National and Commercial - say however that there are facing a major problem with high wage bills and are working towards instituting voluntary retirement in the framework of modernisation and reorganisation efforts in the banking system, due to be announced this week.

--Foreign exchange policies and the successful handling of the drachma's parity by the central bank has convinced the market that the drachma's fluctuations this year will not suprass 2.0 percent and will remain "hard".

--The establishment of a new institutional body which will immediately detect and resolve problems in the capital market is planned by the national economy ministry, according to an interview with ministry secretary-general Apostolos Fotiadis. The new body will be an offshoot of the committee which currently meets under the secretary-general.

--1997 will see radical changes in the banking scene, pundits say. With Theodoros Karatzas at the helm of the National Bank, the bank will see speedy expansion of its portfolio and new financial services and products as well as increasing its share capital by 50 billion drachmas. Share capital increases will also be seen at Alpha Credit (60 billion) and Ergobank (30 billion). The national economy ministry believes that the number of leading banks will shrink in a number of years.

--The state budget will shoulder the burden of 60 billion drachmas of compensation for quake victims in 1996, forcing the government to consider incentives for individuals and businesses to consider insuring for natural disasters. A study is to be undertaken by National Insurance.

--Foreign investors have turned a share of their profits into a capital injection for the Athens bourse, which has already seen some 20 billion drachmas from social security and pension funds placed with more expected. The government, meanwhile, is examining two options of 8.0 percent or 17.0 percent for OTE, Greece's telecoms organisation's, second public offer.
